### Regressors Associated with Transport Mode {#sec-regressors}

```{r}
#| label: multinom-test-inline
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Coefficient table on the log-odds scale: estimates, standard errors, z, p
coef_log <- broom::tidy(multinom_test, conf.int = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::rename(outcome_class = y.level)

# Coefficient table on the odds-ratio scale, with Wald 95% confidence intervals
coef_or <- broom::tidy(multinom_test, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::rename(outcome_class = y.level)

# Non-baseline outcome classes, taken from the data rather than hard coded
non_baseline <- setdiff(levels(test_set$transport_mode), "Car")
class_bike <- grep("Bicycle", non_baseline, value = TRUE)
class_pt   <- grep("Transit", non_baseline, value = TRUE)
class_walk <- grep("Walk",    non_baseline, value = TRUE)

# Pull a single quantity for a given outcome class and term.
# Fails loudly at render time if the class or term name does not match.
get_stat <- function(class, term_name, column, tbl = coef_or) {
  value <- tbl[[column]][tbl$outcome_class == class & tbl$term == term_name]
  if (length(value) != 1) {
    stop("No unique match for outcome class '", class, "' and term '", term_name, "'.")
  }
  value
}

# Numeric formatting that degrades gracefully under quasi-complete separation.
# Returns bare LaTeX, so inline calls are wrapped in $ ... $ in the prose.
fmt_num <- Vectorize(function(x, digits = 3) {
  if (is.na(x)) return("\\text{NA}")
  if (!is.finite(x)) return(paste0(if (x < 0) "-" else "", "\\approx \\infty"))
  if (x != 0 && abs(x) < 10^(-digits)) return("\\approx 0")
  if (abs(x) >= 1e4) {
    e <- floor(log10(abs(x)))
    return(sprintf("%.2f \\times 10^{%d}", x / 10^e, e))
  }
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
})

# p-values: bare form for tables, prefixed form for prose
fmt_pval <- function(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)
}
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste0("= ", fmt_pval(p))
}

# 95% confidence interval on the odds-ratio scale, as a comma-separated pair
fmt_ci <- function(class, term_name, digits = 3) {
  paste0(
    fmt_num(get_stat(class, term_name, "conf.low"), digits), ", ",
    fmt_num(get_stat(class, term_name, "conf.high"), digits)
  )
}
```

The Multinomial Logistic regression model fitted on the test set yields the estimated coefficients above. Note that the estimates and confidence limits in the table of significant coefficients are exponentiated, so that each entry is an odds ratio relative to the baseline category `Car`. A positive value of $\hat{\beta}_j^{(k,\texttt{Car})}$ corresponds to higher values of regressor $j$ being associated with a higher odds of category $k$ relative to `Car`, whereas a negative value of $\hat{\beta}_j^{(k,\texttt{Car})}$ corresponds to lower odds of category $k$ relative to `Car` for higher values of regressor $j$. The significant regression coefficients belong to the `` `r class_pt` `` equation, and we will interpret them below.

**Commute distance:** Commute distance is a significant predictor of choosing public transit over the car ($\text{OR} = `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "commute_distance", "estimate"), 2)`$, $z = `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "commute_distance", "statistic", coef_log), 2)`$, $p `r fmt_p(get_stat(class_pt, "commute_distance", "p.value"))`$, 95% CI: $`r fmt_ci(class_pt, "commute_distance", 2)`$). It has the following interpretation.

> *Holding age, car availability, and weekend commuting status constant, each additional kilometre of one-way commute distance is associated with `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "commute_distance", "estimate"), 2)` times higher odds of choosing public transit over car.*

Although the per-kilometre effect appears modest, it compounds over larger differences in commute length. For example, a commute that is $10$ kilometres longer multiplies the odds of choosing public transit over the car by approximately $`r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "commute_distance", "estimate"), 2)`^{10} \approx `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "commute_distance", "estimate")^10, 1)`$, assuming that age, car availability, and weekend commuting status are held constant.

**Car availability:** Car availability is a significant predictor of choosing public transit over the car ($\text{OR} = `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "has_car_availableYes", "estimate"))`$, $z = `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "has_car_availableYes", "statistic", coef_log), 2)`$, $p `r fmt_p(get_stat(class_pt, "has_car_availableYes", "p.value"))`$, 95% CI: $`r fmt_ci(class_pt, "has_car_availableYes")`$). It has the following interpretation.

> *Holding commute distance, age, and weekend commuting status constant, individuals with a car available have `r fmt_num(get_stat(class_pt, "has_car_availableYes", "estimate"))` times the odds of choosing public transit over the car, relative to individuals without a car available. In other words, car availability is associated with a reduction of approximately `r fmt_num(100 * (1 - get_stat(class_pt, "has_car_availableYes", "estimate")), 1)`% in the odds of choosing public transit over car.*

The remaining rows of the significant coefficients table in the `R` output are artifacts of the quasi-complete separation discussed above and are therefore not interpreted.

## Results

The fitted model can be written as
$$
\log \left( \frac{\Pr(Y_i = k)}{\Pr(Y_i = \text{Car})} \right) = \hat{\beta}_{0}^{(k,\text{Car})} + \hat{\beta}_{1}^{(k,\text{Car})} x_{i,\texttt{distance}} + \hat{\beta}_{2}^{(k,\text{Car})} x_{i,\texttt{age}} + \hat{\beta}_{3}^{(k,\text{Car})}Z_{i,\texttt{car}} + \hat{\beta}_{4}^{(k,\text{Car})} Z_{i,\texttt{weekend}},
$$ {#eq-fitted-model}
where $k$ is one of the non-baseline levels: `` `r class_bike` ``, `` `r class_pt` ``, or `` `r class_walk` ``, and the regressors are denoted as $x_{i,\texttt{distance}}, x_{i,\texttt{age}}, Z_{i,\texttt{car}},$ and $Z_{i,\texttt{weekend}}$.

The estimated intercepts and slope coefficients of the Multinomial Logistic regression model fitted on the test set in @sec-inference are summarized in the three tables below. Every estimate is interpreted relative to the baseline category `Car`, and the $z$ statistics, $p$-values, odds ratios, and $95\%$ Wald confidence intervals are taken directly from the `R` output:

```{r}
#| label: multinom-coef-tables
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

term_order <- c("(Intercept)", "commute_distance", "age",
                "has_car_availableYes", "weekend_commuterYes")
param_labels <- c("(intercept)", "`commute_distance`", "`age`",
                  "`has_car_availableYes`", "`weekend_commuterYes`")

for (k in c(class_bike, class_pt, class_walk)) {

  # Escape underscores and spaces for use inside \text{ } in the parameter symbols
  k_math <- gsub("[ _]", "\\\\_", k)

  cat("**`", k, "` versus `Car`:**\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("| Parameter | Estimate | Std. Error | $z$ | $p$-value | OR | 95% CI |\n")
  cat("|-----------|----------|------------|-----|-----------|-----|--------|\n")

  for (i in seq_along(term_order)) {
    tm <- term_order[i]
    cat(sprintf(
      "| $\\hat{\\beta}_{%d}^{(\\text{%s},\\,\\text{Car})}$ %s | $%s$ | $%s$ | $%s$ | $%s$ | $%s$ | $(%s)$ |\n",
      i - 1L, k_math, param_labels[i],
      fmt_num(get_stat(k, tm, "estimate",   coef_log)),
      fmt_num(get_stat(k, tm, "std.error",  coef_log)),
      fmt_num(get_stat(k, tm, "statistic",  coef_log), 2),
      fmt_pval(get_stat(k, tm, "p.value",   coef_log)),
      fmt_num(get_stat(k, tm, "estimate")),
      fmt_ci(k, tm)
    ))
  }

  cat("\n")
}
```

The `` `r class_bike` `` and `` `r class_pt` `` blocks are estimated on adequate numbers of observations, and within these blocks, `commute_distance` and `has_car_availableYes` in the `` `r class_pt` `` equation are significant at the $5\%$ level. As discussed in @sec-inference, the `` `r class_walk` `` equation and the `weekend_commuterYes` term in the `` `r class_bike` `` equation suffer from quasi-complete separation; the resulting extreme coefficient magnitudes paired with astronomical standard errors drive the associated $z$-statistics toward zero and the $p$-values toward one, which is a symptom of a maximum likelihood estimate that does not exist rather than genuine null effects.

### Prediction 

Now we will fit the Multinomial Logistic regression model on the train set, and predict on the held-out test set. The confusion matrix and performance metrics are reported below.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## R Code

```{.r}
# Fit the model on the train set
multinom_fit <- multinom(transport_mode ~ age + commute_distance + has_car_available + weekend_commuter, data = train_set)

# Predict on the test set using the fitted model
y_pred <- predict(multinom_fit, newdata = test_set)

# Compute confusion matrix
mode_levels <- c("Car", "Bicycle", "Public_Transit", "Walking")
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(factor(y_pred, levels = mode_levels),
                              factor(test_set$transport_mode, levels = mode_levels))

# Visualise
cm_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(conf_matrix$table))
colnames(cm_df) <- c("Predicted", "Actual", "Freq")

# Order axes so the main diagonal (correct matches) runs top-left to bottom-right
cm_df$Predicted <- factor(cm_df$Predicted, levels = levels(cm_df$Predicted))
cm_df$Actual    <- factor(cm_df$Actual,    levels = rev(levels(cm_df$Actual)))

cm_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), color = "black", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#2171b5") +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix (Test Set)",
       x = "Predicted label", y = "True label") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13)
```

## Python Code

```{.python}
# Factorize the response and set the baseline model
train_set["transport_mode"] = pd.Categorical(
    train_set["transport_mode"],
    categories=["Car", "Bicycle", "Public_Transit", "Walking"],
    ordered=False
)

# Design matrix and response
y = train_set["transport_mode"]
X = train_set[["age", "commute_distance", "has_car_available", "weekend_commuter"]]

# Add intercept
X = sm.add_constant(X)

# Convert categorical variables to numeric codes for statsmodels MNLogit
X_numeric = X.copy()
for col in ['has_car_available', 'weekend_commuter']:
    X_numeric[col] = X_numeric[col].cat.codes

# Fit Multinomial Logistic regression
model = sm.MNLogit(y, X_numeric)
multinom_fit = model.fit()

# Predict on the test set using the fitted model
test_set["transport_mode"] = pd.Categorical(
  test_set["transport_mode"],
  categories=["Car", "Bicycle", "Public_Transit", "Walking"],
    ordered=False
)
y_test = test_set["transport_mode"]
X_test = test_set[["age", "commute_distance", "has_car_available", "weekend_commuter"]]
X_test = sm.add_constant(X_test)
X_test_num = X_test.copy()
for col in ['has_car_available', 'weekend_commuter']:
    X_test_num[col] = X_test_num[col].cat.codes
y_pred_test = multinom_fit.predict(X_test_num).idxmax(axis=1)

# Confusion matrix
labels = y_test.cat.categories
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test.cat.codes, y_pred_test, labels=range(len(labels)))
disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm,
                              display_labels=y_test.cat.categories)
disp.plot(cmap="Blues")
disp.ax_.set_title("Confusion Matrix (Test Set)")
fig = disp.figure_
fig.tight_layout()
fig
```

## R Code

```{.r}
# Compute the performance metrics
overall_accuracy <- conf_matrix$overall['Accuracy']
macro_recall <- mean(conf_matrix$byClass[,"Recall"], na.rm = TRUE)
macro_f1 <- mean(conf_matrix$byClass[,"F1"], na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Overall Accuracy:", round(overall_accuracy, 3), "\n")
cat("Macro Recall:", round(macro_recall, 3), "\n")
cat("Macro F1:", round(macro_f1, 3), "\n")
```

## Python Code

```{.python}
# Compute the performance metrics
acc = accuracy_score(y_test.cat.codes, y_pred_test)
recall = recall_score(y_test.cat.codes, y_pred_test, average='macro')
# Average F1 only over the classes the model actually predicts, so a
# never-predicted class (undefined precision) is dropped rather than
# counted as 0 — matching caret's byClass F1 with na.rm = TRUE in the R tab.
predicted_labels = np.unique(y_pred_test)
f1 = f1_score(y_test.cat.codes, y_pred_test, labels=predicted_labels, average='macro')
print(f"Overall Accuracy: {acc:.3f}")
print(f"Macro Recall: {recall:.3f}")
```

:::

On the test set, the model achieves an overall accuracy of **`r 100.0*round(overall_accuracy, 3)`%**, a macro recall of **`r 100.0*round(macro_recall, 3)`%**, and a macro F1 score of **`r 100.0*round(macro_f1, 3)`%**. 

The `Car` and `Public Transit` classes are predicted most reliably with recalls of $82.9\%$ and $64.7\%$ respectively. On the other hand, the observations corresponding to minority classes (`Bicycle` and `Walking`) in the test set are all misclassified as `Car` or `Public Transit`. Among the seven `Bicycle` observations in the test set, six are misclassified as `Car` and one is misclassified as `Public_Transit`. For the two `Walking` observations in the test set, one is misclassified as `Car` and one is misclassified as `Public_Transit`. 

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Class Imbalance and Prediction
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
The absence of `Bicycle` and `Walking` predictions follows from the structure of the maximum likelihood solution under class imbalance. Differentiating the log-likelihood function in @eq-log-likelihood-multinomial with respect to the intercept $\beta_0^{(j,1)}$ of a non-baseline category $j$ and setting the partial derivative to zero yields the following equation:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{p}_{i,j} = \sum_{i=1}^n y_{i,j} = n_j,
$$

where $n_j$ is the number of observations in category $j$ in the train set. Consequently, the fitted probabilities of each category average exactly its sample proportion in the train set, which is roughly $2.4\%$ for `Bicycle` and less than $1\%$ for `Walking`. Since the classification rule assigns each observation to the category with the highest fitted probability, a minority category is predicted only when the regressors raise its fitted probability well above its small sample proportion, and the estimated slope coefficients do not produce a shift of that magnitude for any regressor values observed in the test set. Neither `Bicycle` nor `Walking` therefore ever attains the maximum fitted probability, due to which these minority classes are not predicted at all in the test set.
::::
:::

Now let's use the upsampled model (`multinom_fit_balanced`) from @sec-estimation to predict on the held-out test set. The confusion matrix and performance metrics are reported below.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## R Code
```{.r}
# Predict on the test set using the fitted multinom_fit_balanced model
y_pred <- predict(multinom_fit_balanced, newdata = test_set)

# Compute confusion matrix
mode_levels <- c("Car", "Bicycle", "Public_Transit", "Walking")
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(factor(y_pred, levels = mode_levels),
                              factor(test_set$transport_mode, levels = mode_levels))

# Visualise
cm_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(conf_matrix$table))
colnames(cm_df) <- c("Predicted", "Actual", "Freq")

# Order axes so the main diagonal (correct matches) runs top-left to
# bottom-right: Predicted increases left -> right (Car -> Walking), and
# Actual increases top -> bottom (Car -> Walking). ggplot draws the first
# factor level at the bottom of the y-axis, so we reverse Actual's levels to
# place "Car" at the top.
cm_df$Predicted <- factor(cm_df$Predicted, levels = levels(cm_df$Predicted))
cm_df$Actual    <- factor(cm_df$Actual,    levels = rev(levels(cm_df$Actual)))

cm_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), color = "black", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#2171b5") +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix (Test Set)",
       x = "Predicted label", y = "True label") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13)
```

## Storytelling

To complete the data science workflow, let's step back from the coefficients, tests, and confusion matrices, and focus on how the results can be interpreted and applied in practice. This final stage, storytelling, is where statistical output is translated into insights that support real world decision making.

In this case study, the Multinomial Logistic regression model helps us understand how commute distance, age, car availability, and weekend commuting status relate to an individual's primary mode of transport, an outcome with four unordered categories: `Car`, `Public Transit`, `Bicycle`, and `Walking`. We will distill the key takeaways from the analysis and discuss what they imply for commuters, transportation planners, and policy makers.

### Key Insights From the Model

Car availability and commute distance are the two most consistently significant regressors across both the imbalanced and upsampled models. Having access to a car is associated with lower odds of using public transit instead of driving; the corresponding effect for cycling is not statistically significant, so car access alone does not appear to explain the choice to bike in this dataset. Commute distance moves the odds of public transit and cycling in opposite directions relative to driving, such that each additional kilometre increases the odds of choosing public transit over the car, while decreasing the odds of cycling over the car. This matches the intuition that the car and public transit become the practical options once a commute gets long, while cycling remains attractive mainly over short distances.

Age and weekend commuting status tell a more conditional story. On the original, imbalanced training data, neither regressor reaches statistical significance for most categories, largely because the sample contains too few cyclists and walkers to estimate their effects precisely. Once the minority classes are upsampled, both regressors become significant predictors of `Walking`, and age additionally becomes significant for `Bicycle`: older individuals and weekend commuters are more likely to walk than drive, once the class imbalance no longer masks the effect. This is a useful reminder that failing to reject $H_0$ is not the same as confirming $H_0$ because a lack of significance can potentially reflect insufficient data rather than a genuinely null effect for rare categories.

Some estimates need a caveat rather than a substantive interpretation. The test set contains only one `Walking` observation and five `Bicycle` observations, none of the latter being weekend commuters, so the test set model suffers from complete separation. In R, the `weekend_commuter` effect for `Bicycle` and several `Walking` coefficients are flagged as significant with implausibly large or near-zero odds ratios, standard errors of essentially zero, and extreme test statistics. In Python, `statsmodels` assigns the same terms enormous standard errors and $p$-values near 1, and reports that the fit did not fully converge. None of this is evidence about the true effects; the terms are simply not identifiable from the available data. Analysts should flag this kind of estimate rather than interpret it, and should be cautious of near-zero or implausibly large odds ratios whenever a category is small.

As a predictive tool, the model favours the categories it has seen the most of. The confusion matrices for both the training and test sets show noticeably stronger performance for `Car` and `Public Transit`, the two dominant categories, than for `Bicycle` and `Walking`. Upsampling helps the model learn the minority classes better during estimation, but it cannot manufacture additional information at prediction time, so macro-averaged recall and F1 remain modest even after balancing. The model is best used as a tool for understanding how commute distance, car availability, age, and weekend habits relate to travel mode choice, rather than as a precise classifier for the least common commuting behaviours.

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Using the Results Responsibly
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
It is important to remember that this analysis is associational, not causal. The model does not prove that changing someone's commute distance or car access would, on its own, change how they travel; it shows that, in this dataset, these regressors are consistently linked to the mode people choose once other measured factors are accounted for.

Nevertheless, the results provide a useful evidence-based starting point for discussion. They help identify which regressors are most closely linked to travel mode choice, and which associations, such as age and weekend commuting for the rarer categories, may only become visible with more balanced or more abundant data. For transportation planners, this kind of insight can help prioritize where infrastructure investment, such as bike lanes or improved transit access, is likely to shift commuting patterns the most.
::::
:::
